questions.q: How many vowel sounds does modern Israeli Hebrew have?
questions.why: Five: a, e, i, o, u. There are about ten signs to write them, because the system was designed for a pronunciation that still had long and short vowels. Israeli Hebrew dropped the length and kept the signs.

questions.q: Which two signs both say the vowel a?
questions.why: קָמָץ and פַּתָּח are both /a/, as צֵירֵי and סֶגּוֹל are both /e/ and קוּבּוּץ and שׁוּרוּק are both /u/. Reading them is easy because each pair gives one instruction; writing them is not, which is why you learn the spelling with the word.

questions.q: Which vowel sign is under the first letter of בַּיִת?
questions.why: It is a פַּתָּח, a single horizontal stroke. A קָמָץ has a small tail hanging under that stroke, and in modern speech the two say exactly the same thing, so they are told apart by shape and never by ear.

questions.q: Which sign usually marks no vowel at all?
questions.why: שְׁוָוא is two dots stacked vertically. In the middle of a word it is silence, and at the start of a word it is a faint /e/. An English speaker's instinct is to insert a full vowel, and that extra vowel is what sounds foreign.

questions.q: Put these sign names in the order of the sounds a, e, i, o, u.
questions.why: One sign per sound, in the order a, e, i, o, u. Each of these has a twin that says the same thing: פַּתָּח for a, סֶגּוֹל for e, and קוּבּוּץ for u. That is ten signs doing five jobs.

questions.q: Type the Hebrew word for a market, read /shuk/.
questions.why: The u is a שׁוּרוּק, a ו with a dot in its belly. Compare a חוֹלָם מָלֵא, which is the same ו with the dot sitting above it and to the left: the position of one dot is the whole difference between /u/ and /o/.

questions.q: Type the Hebrew word for a city, read /ir/.
questions.why: The i is a חִירִיק, one dot under the letter, and here it has a י after it to carry the sound once the points come off. The opening ע is silent: the word starts on the vowel.
Books, /sfarim/. The shva under the ס is silence, so the word opens with a consonant cluster and has two syllables, not three. Saying se-fa-rim inserts a vowel that is not written and not there.
The sign under the א is a חֲטָף פַּתָּח, a shva with a patakh beside it, and it is a very short /a/ rather than a full one. The gutturals א ה ח ע take these compounds because they resist a bare shva.

questions.q: Why do א, ה, ח and ע take a חֲטָף instead of a plain שְׁוָוא?
choices: They are gutturals and resist a bare shva
They are the only letters that can start a word
A shva cannot be written under a wide letter
They are silent, so they need a sign of their own
questions.why: The four gutturals want something to lean on, so the shva is compounded with a vowel: חֲטָף פַּתָּח, חֲטָף סֶגּוֹל, חֲטָף קָמָץ. You never choose one, it belongs to the spelling of the word; you only need to read it as a short vowel.
Friends, /khaverim/. A חֲטָף פַּתָּח under the ח, a צֵירֵי under the ב, and the stress on the last syllable. The short opening vowel is what keeps it from sounding like a full kha.

questions.q: Type the Hebrew word for truth, read /emet/.
questions.why: Under the א is a חֲטָף סֶגּוֹל, a very short /e/, and under the מ a full סֶגּוֹל. The same sound written two ways in one three-letter word, because the guttural takes the compound and the ordinary letter does not.

questions.q: In the word כָּל, meaning all, how is the kamatz read?
questions.why: This is a קָמָץ קָטָן, the one kamatz that says /o/: כָּל is /kol/. It belongs to a small and learnable set of words, so meet each one as it comes rather than trying to predict it.

questions.q: Why can you not work out by ear whether a word is written with a קָמָץ or a פַּתָּח, and what follows from that for a learner?
a: Because Israeli Hebrew merged the two: both are /a/, and the historical difference in length is gone. So listening can never tell you which to write. What follows is that you learn a spelling together with the word, you do not try to derive it, and you spend your effort on reading the points rather than producing them, since almost nothing outside a dictionary or a children's book is pointed anyway.
questions.why: The same applies to צֵירֵי against סֶגּוֹל and to קוּבּוּץ against שׁוּרוּק. Recognising that the writing system is finer than the sound system saves a lot of wasted effort trying to hear a distinction that no longer exists.
